title: Young and dynamic
caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 2865, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2865 · constellation Hydra · about 100 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A faint halo surrounds NGC 2865, an elliptical galaxy just over 100 million light-years away in Hydra, the Sea Serpent. John Herschel discovered it in 1835, and Judy Schmidt entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

Elliptical galaxies are usually full of old, dying stars, but NGC 2865 is fairly young and lively. It has a rapidly rotating disc of young stars and metal-rich gas, and an unusually large number of young stars for its type. That suggests a starburst swept through the whole galaxy about one billion years ago.

The starburst was set off by a merger. A spiral galaxy much like the Milky Way combined with an elliptical about three times its mass, the forerunner of NGC 2865. Fresh gas from the spiral revived the ageing elliptical, and it went on to form several new generations of stars. The halo is also a product of that merger. It is cold gas torn from the spiral, now forming an almost closed shell around the galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.42 x 3.29 arcminutes) and distance (100 million light years), the frame spans roughly 99,000 × 96,000 light-years. Its light set out about 100 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 2865 in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The halo of gas is very faint, and Hubble's exposures reveal far more of it than an eye at a telescope could.
